diet.note: No preserved stomach contents; diet inferred. It may have eaten small reptiles, mammals or insects.

timeRange.note: Early Tithonian, from PBDB occurrence ages for A. lithographica. All Archaeopteryx specimens come from the Altmühltal, Mörnsheim and Painten formations of Bavaria; the oldest, from the earliest Tithonian Painten Formation, is referred only to the genus (Rauhut et al. 2018).

massKg.note: Earlier estimates for known specimens range from 200 to 600 g; Erickson et al. (2009) estimate an adult (asymptotic) mass of about 895 to 928 g, because none of the known specimens appears fully grown.

text.en: Archaeopteryx is a famous bird-like dinosaur from the Late Jurassic of southern Germany, about 149 to 145 million years ago. About the size of a magpie, it had broad feathered wings, but unlike modern birds it also had sharp teeth and a long bony tail. Its fossils come from limestone that formed in a lagoon. Found in 1861, two years after Darwin's On the Origin of Species, it seemed to support the idea that birds evolved from dinosaurs.
Fossil pigment structures in an isolated Archaeopteryx feather suggest it was black, with 95% probability.
Archaeopteryx grew slowly: its bones suggest it took about two to three years to reach adult size, about three times slower than living precocial birds.

alt.en: The original Berlin specimen of Archaeopteryx lithographica, a fossil skeleton with feather impressions in a limestone slab.

uncertain.note: Archaeopteryx is usually placed at the base of Avialae, but one analysis (Xu et al. 2011) moved it into Deinonychosauria, with only weak support.
Archaeopteryx specimens vary a lot in limb proportions and teeth; Rauhut et al. (2018) discuss whether they belong to one species or a 'species flock', so not every specimen may be A. lithographica.
